summary: Defines a MIB for controlling a Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement meter, especially for specifying which flows to measure. It also provides an efficient way to retrieve flow data from the meter using SNMP. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the SNMP objects for a traffic flow meter: a device that watches network traffic, groups the packets into flows, and counts what each flow carried. It covers how to tell the meter which flows to watch, and how to read the counts back efficiently.

subtitle: The SNMP interface for configuring a network traffic meter and efficiently reading the flows it counts.

tldr.problem: A network needs to know which traffic flows cross it and how much each carries, and the operator needs a way to tell a meter which flows to watch and a way to get the counts back without thousands of SNMP exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the FLOW-METER-MIB: control tables for loading rule sets and managing readers and managers, a table of flow records, a table of rules that say which packets to count, and a data package table that returns several flow attributes in a single object.
tldr.outcome: A meter reader can fetch exactly the attributes it wants for the flows that changed since its last pass. The document is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2064.

today: RFC 2720 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1999. It obsoleted RFC 2064 and has not been obsoleted since. It defines the SNMP interface for an RTFM traffic meter; the measurement architecture it belongs to is described in a separate document.

sections.title: What the Meter MIB Is For
sections.content:
Traffic Flow Measurement seeks to provide a well-defined method for gathering traffic flow information from networks and internetworks. The Realtime Traffic Flow Measurement working group produced a measurement architecture for this, which defines three entities: meters, which observe network traffic flows and build up a table of flow data records for them; meter readers, which collect traffic flow data from meters; and managers, which oversee the operation of meters and meter readers.

This memo defines the SNMP management information for a Traffic Flow Meter. The MIB is 'basic' in the sense that it provides more than enough information for everyday traffic measurement, and it can be extended by adding new attributes as required. All the objects are registered in a single subtree within the mib-2 namespace, under an SMI Network Management MGMT Code of 40, that is flowMIB OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= mib-2 40. They are for use in network devices that may perform a PDU forwarding or monitoring function.

The module is compliant with SMIv2. The RTFM Meter MIB was first produced and tested using SNMPv1, and was converted into SNMPv2 following the guidelines of RFC 1908.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture has three roles: the meter watches the traffic and counts it, meter readers fetch the counts, and managers tell the meter what to watch. This document defines the SNMP objects that let those three talk to each other.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organised
sections.content:
The MIB is organised in four parts: control, data, rules and conformance statements. The rules implement the set of packet-matching actions described in the RTFM architecture document, and in addition they provide for BASIC-style subroutines, allowing a network manager to dramatically reduce the number of rules required to monitor a large network.

Traffic flows are identified by a set of attributes for each of their end-points. The attributes include network addresses for each layer of the network protocol stack, and 'subscriber ids', which may be used to identify an accountable entity for the flow. The conformance statements are set out as defined in RFC 2580, and they explain what must be implemented in a meter that claims to conform to this MIB.

All the MIB variables are set up to allow multiple independent meter readers to work properly, which means the flow table indexes are stateless. An alternative approach would have been to 'snapshot' the flow table, which would mean the meter readers would have to be synchronized. The stateless approach means that two meter readers will never return exactly the same set of traffic counts, but over long periods, for example 15-minute collections over a day, the discrepancies are acceptable. If a true snapshot is needed, it can be achieved by switching to an identical rule set with a different RuleSet number, so asynchronous collections may be regarded as a useful generalization of synchronized ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has four parts: what to configure, the flow records themselves, the rules that decide what to count, and a statement of what a conforming meter must implement. The flow table is deliberately not snapshot-based, so several readers can collect from one meter at the same time.

sections.title: The Control Tables
sections.content:
The control variables are the minimum set required for a meter reader, and their number has been whittled down as experience has been gained with the MIB implementation. A few of them are 'general', in that they control the overall behaviour of the meter; these are set by a single 'master' manager, and no other manager should try to change their values. The decision about which manager is the master has to be made by the network operations personnel responsible, and the MIB does not define any interaction between managers.

Three further groups of control variables are arranged into tables in the same way as in the RMON2 MIB. Rule Set Info: before downloading a RuleSet, a manager must create a row in the flowRuleSetInfoTable and set its flowRuleInfoSize to a value large enough to hold the RuleSet. When the rule set is ready, the manager must set flowRuleInfoRulesReady to 'true', indicating that the rule set is ready for use but not yet running. Meter Reader Info: a reader wishing to collect data reliably for all flows from a RuleSet should first create a row in the flowReaderInfoTable with flowReaderRuleSet set to that RuleSet's index in the flowRuleSetInfoTable. It should write that row's flowReaderLastTime object each time it starts a collection pass through the flow table. The meter will not recover a flow's memory until every meter reader holding a row for that flow's RuleSet has collected the flow's data.

Manager Info: a manager wishing to run a RuleSet in the meter must create a row in the flowManagerInfo table, specifying the desired RuleSet to run and its corresponding 'standby' RuleSet, if one is desired. A current RuleSet is 'running' if its flowManagerRunningStandby value is false(2), and a standby RuleSet is 'running' if that value is true(1). Times within the meter are in terms of its Uptime, that is centiseconds since the meter started. For meters implemented as self-contained SNMP agents this is the same as sysUptime, but that may not be true for meters implemented as subagents, so managers can read the meter's Uptime when necessary, for example to set a TimeFilter value, by setting flowReaderLastTime and then reading its new value. A further table, flowInterfaceTable, holds per-interface information: flowInterfaceSampleRate sets the parameter N for statistical counting, where a rate of 1 counts all packets and a rate of 0 makes the meter ignore the interface, and flowInterfaceLostPackets counts the packets the meter has lost because it could not keep up with the traffic volume.
sections.plainLanguage: Loading rules and running them takes three kinds of row. A manager allocates space for a rule set and says when it is ready, a reader registers itself so the meter knows not to discard data before it has been collected, and the manager names which rule set is running and which is standing by to take over.

sections.title: Reading Flow Data Efficiently
sections.content:
To retrieve flow data one could simply do a linear scan of the flow table. That would certainly work, but it would require a lot of protocol exchanges. To reduce the overhead, the flow table uses a TimeFilter variable, defined as a textual convention in the RMON2 MIB, so that a reader can ask only for rows that changed since a given time.

As an alternative, the MIB provides a view of the flow table called the flowDataPackageTable. This is logically a four-dimensional array, subscripted by package selector, RuleSet, activity time and starting flow number. The package selector is a sequence of bytes specifying a list of flow attributes, encoded as a sequence of octets each containing a FlowAttribute number, preceded by an octet giving the length of the sequence, not counting the length octet; a valid selector must contain at least one attribute.

A data package, as returned by the meter, is a sequence of values for the attributes specified in its selector, encoded using the Basic Encoding Rules, and it lets a meter reader retrieve all the attribute values it requires in a single MIB object. Used together with SNMPv2's GetBulk request, this allows a reader to scan the flow table and upload a specified set of attribute values for flows that have changed since the last reading and that were created by a specified rule set. The RFC gives the object identifier to use: to retrieve a package containing values for attributes 11, 18 and 29, for a flow in RuleSet 7, with flow index 3447, the reader GETs the package whose object identifier is flowPackageData . 3.11.18.29 . 7. 0 . 3447, and to get the package for the next such flow that had been active since time 12345, it GETNEXTs the package whose object identifier is flowPackageData . 3.11.18.29 . 7. 12345 . 3447.
sections.plainLanguage: Walking the whole flow table would need thousands of requests. Two shortcuts avoid that: a time filter that skips rows that have not changed, and a data package that packs several attributes of one flow into a single object, which can be fetched in bulk.

sections.title: The Flow Data Table
sections.content:
flowDataTable is the list of all flows being measured, and each row is indexed by flowDataRuleSet, flowDataTimeMark and flowDataIndex, so a reader can ask for the flows created by one rule set. The row describes both ends of the flow. For the source there is the interface, the adjacent type, address and mask, the peer type, address and mask, and the transport type, address and mask; the destination has the matching set of objects. A flow also carries a PDU scale and an octet scale, and the counters flowDataToOctets, flowDataToPDUs, flowDataFromOctets and flowDataFromPDUs, which count octets and protocol data units in each direction. flowDataFirstTime and flowDataLastActiveTime give the activity times.

Three further objects identify the end points: flowDataSourceSubscriberID, flowDataDestSubscriberID and flowDataSessionID. A set of six objects classifies the flow: the source class, destination class and overall class, and the source kind, destination kind and overall kind. The class and kind attributes are computed values that rule actions can set and that rules can then test.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row of the flow table describes one conversation: the addresses at each layer of the protocol stack on both sides, how much data went each way, when it was active, and any subscriber or session identifiers assigned to it.

sections.title: The Rule Table
sections.content:
flowRuleTable contains all the RuleSets that the meter may use, and the running ones are indicated by the entries in the meter's flowManagerInfoTable. Several RuleSets can be held in a meter so that the manager can change the running RuleSets easily, for example with time of day. A manager may not change the rules in any RuleSet currently referenced in the flowManagerInfoTable, either as current or as standby. Although an individual rule within a RuleSet could be modified, the RFC says it is much safer to download a complete new RuleSet.

Each row of the rule table is indexed by flowRuleSet and flowRuleIndex, and holds five fields. flowRuleSelector names the attribute to be matched, with null(0) a special case whose rules always succeed. flowRuleMask is the initial mask used to compute the desired value, and if the mask is zero the rule's test always succeeds. flowRuleMatchedValue is the value to be matched for equality: if the attribute chosen by the selector, logically ANDed with the mask, equals this value, processing continues with the action given by flowRuleAction, and otherwise processing moves to the next entry in the rule table. The action is an opcode for the meter's Packet Matching Engine. flowRuleParameter, an integer from 0 to 65535, supplies extra information; most of the actions use it to specify which rule to execute after the rule's test has failed.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule picks an attribute, masks it, and compares the result with a value. If they match, the action field says what to do next and the parameter says where to go; if they do not match, the meter moves on to the next rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects defined in this MIB have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments: support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. Many objects may hold sensitive information, including all the objects in the Control Group, because they control access to meter resources, and those in the Flow Table, because they hold the collected traffic flow data. It is therefore important to control even GET access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP. Not all versions of SNMP provide features for such a secure environment: SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may GET or SET the objects in this MIB. The RFC recommends the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model, and notes that it is then the customer's or user's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity to give access only to principals with legitimate rights.

For the meter itself, the RFC says the MIB describes how a meter is controlled and how flow data is retrieved from it, which is essentially an application using SNMP between cooperating hosts and does not in itself have inherent security risks. Since however the traffic flow data can be extremely valuable, sensible precautions must be taken to keep the meter and its data secure, and in particular an attacker must not be permitted to write any of the meter's variables. The RFC lists three ways to restrict control access: physical separation, so that meters and meter readers sit on a separate, carefully controlled network; application-layer security, using community strings with SNMPv2c for a minimal level or the SNMPv3 security models where stronger security is needed; and lower-layer security, protecting access with encryption at the network layer, for example running SNMP to the meter through an encrypted TCP tunnel. A meter may sensibly use separate network interfaces for control and for metering, so that the control network carries no user traffic and the metering interfaces ignore attempts to take control of the meter.

Users should also consider attempts to circumvent a meter, which are denial-of-service attacks on the metering interfaces. A port scan attack sends packets to a very large number of address and port pairs, each of which creates a new flow in the meter, until the meter recognises a 'flood' condition and probably stops creating new flows, so meters should be able to recover from flood conditions as soon as possible after they occur. A counter wrap attack sends enough packets to make the counters in a flow wrap several times between meter readings, so the counts come out artificially low; the change to 64-bit counters in this MIB reduces this problem significantly. Reading meters often enough to prevent them being flooded reduces the severity of both attacks, and the resulting flow data will contain a record of the attacking packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of risk matter here. The first is that someone writes to the meter and changes what it counts, so writes have to be locked down and the SNMPv3 security features used. The second is that someone floods the meter with traffic so it stops measuring, or wraps its counters so the numbers come out too low.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2064
sections.content:
The first version of the Meter MIB was published as RFC 2064 in January 1997. The RFC lists the most significant changes since then. Textual conventions are used more heavily to describe the various types of addresses used by the meter. Computed attributes such as FlowClass and FlowKind may now be tested, which allows these variables to store information during packet matching, and a new attribute, MatchingStoD, has been added, whose value is 1 while a packet is being matched with its addresses in source-to-destination order.

Flood mode is now a read-write variable, and setting it to false(2) switches the meter out of flood mode and back to normal operation. Several variables have been added to the RuleSet, Reader and Manager tables to give more effective control of the meter's activities.

In the flow table, 64-bit counters are used for octet and PDU counts, which reduces the problems caused by the wrap-around of 32-bit counters in earlier versions, and flowDataRuleSet is now used as an index to the flow table, so a reader can collect only the rows created by a specified RuleSet. The data package table is entirely new: it lets a reader retrieve values for a list of attributes from a flow as a single object, a BER-encoded sequence, which is an efficient way to recover flow data, particularly with SNMP GetBulk requests. Earlier versions had a 'Column Activity Table', and using it was difficult to collect all data for a flow efficiently in a single SNMP request. That table is deprecated, as is flowManagerCounterWrap.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the first version, the counters have been widened to 64 bits so that they wrap far less often, the flow table gained an index by rule set, and the data package table replaced an older table that was awkward to read in bulk.

viz.caption: The five fields that make up one rule

items.title: flowRuleSelector
items.text: The attribute to match. A selector of null(0) always succeeds.

items.title: flowRuleMask
items.text: The mask used to compute the value. A mask of zero always succeeds.

items.title: flowRuleMatchedValue
items.text: The value compared with the masked attribute. No match means moving on to the next rule.

items.title: flowRuleAction
items.text: An opcode telling the meter's packet matching engine what to do.

items.title: flowRuleParameter
items.text: Extra information for the action, usually which rule to run if the test fails.
